query_wording: Across recently closed urban transport projects in South Asia, what recurring implementation lessons appear in completion reports?

turns.user: Across recently closed urban transport projects in South Asia, what recurring implementation lessons appear in completion reports?

expected_sources.role: Closed urban transport projects in South Asia, newest closing first
expected_sources.note: Most recently closed South Asia transport projects are highways, rural roads or freight; projects focused on urban transport with ICRs closed in 2016-2019.

expected_sources.role: Bangladesh Clean Air and Sustainable Environment Project, with Dhaka urban transport components (closed 2019-03-31)

text: Coverage: completion reports of three South Asian operations with urban transport at their core: India Sustainable Urban Transport Project (SUTP, P110371, closed March 2018, ICR 2019), India Mumbai Urban Transport Project-2A (MUTP-2A, P113028, closed December 2016, ICR 2017) and Bangladesh Clean Air and Sustainable Environment (CASE, P098151, closed March 2019, ICR 2019; Dhaka traffic and transport components). 'Recently closed' is a stretch: South Asia transport projects closed since 2020 are mostly highways, rural roads and freight corridors, not urban transport.

1. Institutional ownership and coordination decide outcomes. SUTP: city agencies' commitment wavered (Pune cancelled at the start; problems in Indore and Pimpri-Chinchwad), and a stronger state government role stabilized implementation, so future projects should engage states (ICR pp. 32); BRT needs a dedicated, multifunctional nodal entity such as an SPV - Hubli-Dharwad's HDBRTSCo worked, Pimpri-Chinchwad without one did not (pp. 32-33). MUTP-2A: MRVC implemented works on a railway operated by others; the Bank's convening power and restructurings helped resolve coordination issues such as trespass control, and agency mandates should be shaped for long-term sustainability (pp. 34-35). CASE: an integrated cross-sector approach needs mechanisms for inter-agency coordination, and stakeholder engagement within government should be planned at design to avoid delays such as the slow handover of traffic signals to the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (pp. 35-36).

2. Plan operations, not just civil works. SUTP: cities prepared for operating BRT and ITS only as works ended, despite advice years earlier; BRT and ITS realize value only with service plans and organizational capacity (p. 33).

3. Technical and interface risks need explicit preparation. MUTP-2A: developing a new rolling-stock configuration for legacy platforms caused design-approval delays and should be treated differently from buying proven designs (p. 35).

4. Choose attributable indicators. MUTP-2A's targets assumed a parallel project (MUTP-2B) and were probably too ambitious; use indicators strongly attributable to the project and restructure them if needed (p. 35).
5. Capacity building pays off when hands-on. SUTP's practitioner-oriented training and guidance with national workshops built a community of urban mobility practitioners (p. 32).
Recurring themes across the three: coordination among many agencies, the need for a clear lead entity, and preparing for operations and stakeholder buy-in early.

right_sources: Reads ICRs of at least two closed South Asian urban transport projects (the reference set or other qualifying ones).
grounded: Each lesson is cited to an ICR and page; lessons are the ICRs' own, not generic advice.
complete: Identifies lessons that recur across projects, not only per-project lists.
scoped: States the projects read, their closing dates, and how 'recently closed' and 'urban transport' were interpreted.

notes: If newer South Asian urban transport ICRs appear (e.g. Karachi or Dhaka BRT operations), the judge should accept them if grounded.
